source: Abstract: In this work, two novel methods are introduced to tackle the multi-organ segmentation using deep learning. Both proposed techniques exploit the idea of leveraging multiple input planes as parallel channels on which different supervision schemes can be defined so that information flow among such representations can better handle ambiguous signals coming from partial or irrelevant annotations (semi supervision) and also boost generalization to test images with occluded or rotated organs relative to training data. Specifically, instead of operating only in the spatial domain, co-training in our case is effectively achieved along both planes thanks to the combination between a convolutional autoencoder applied to extracting features from RGB channels (which mainly capture shape variations)and the application of 3D ResNets acting on a T2w/FLAIR subtraction volume used to convey anatomical details. Such components allow us to efficiently represent both appearance and geometry through complementary domains providing important contributions in terms of performance over standard approaches based on unimodal channels and end-to-end architectures. Our results show marked improvements w.r.t seminal MICCAI publications obtained applying similar algorithms. A quantitative comparison carried out on five public datasets including brain tumor slices demonstrates that by simply modifying the backbone architecture we exceed state-of-the-art scores achieving results comparable with human experts without the need for any form of interactive fine tuning.
text: This study introduces two innovative methods for multi-organ segmentation using deep learning. Both techniques utilize the concept of leveraging multiple input planes as parallel channels, allowing different supervision schemes to be defined for each plane. This approach enables the information flow to better handle ambiguous signals from partial or irrelevant annotations (semi-supervision) and to enhance generalization to test images with occluded or rotated organs. The study combines a convolutional autoencoder for RGB channels to extract features and a 3D ResNet for T2w/FLAIR subtraction to convey anatomical details. This approach enables the efficient representation of both appearance and geometry using complementary domains, providing significant performance improvements over standard methods. The study's results show marked improvements over seminal MICCAI publications, with a quantitative comparison on five public datasets demonstrating that the proposed methods exceed state-of-the-art scores, achieving results comparable to human experts with a simple modification of the backbone architecture.

source: I have been binge-watching Bob Ross videos lately and I must say, I absolutely love his soothing voice and calming presence. He is truly a talented artist and watching him create beautiful landscapes is incredibly inspiring. However, there is one minor issue that I have noticed with his paintings. While I appreciate the simplicity and accessibility of his techniques, sometimes I feel like the end results can be a bit too similar. Don't get me wrong, I love his signature style with the happy little trees and fluffy clouds, but after watching several episodes, the paintings start to blend together for me. I would love to see him experiment with different subjects or styles to mix things up and keep the audience engaged. Nonetheless, this is just a tiny gripe compared to the overall joy and relaxation I get from watching Bob Ross paint.

The abstract for the academic paper titled "UXNet: Searching Multi-level Feature Aggregation for 3D Medical Image Segmentation" could be:

Medical image segmentation plays a pivotal role in clinical analysis and computer-aided diagnosis. Unlike 2D images, 3D medical images possess more informative structures and afford robust segmentation. However, how to effectively explore the rich information in 3D medical images remains a challenge. In this paper, we present a novel deep learning architecture, called UXNet, for 3D medical image segmentation. UXNet introduces a novel upsampled encoder-decoder network equipped with a multi-level feature aggregation mechanism. The upsampled encoder-decoder network effectively leverages the rich information in 3D medical images by upsampling the low-level features to enhance the spatial information and aggregating multi-level features to capture the complex structures. Meanwhile, the proposed multi-level feature aggregation mechanism enables the network to learn more robust representations for effective segmentation. Extensive experiments on three benchmark datasets, including ISLES2017, LLC and SYNAPSE-BREAST-CT, demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of UXNet compared with the state-of-the-art methods. The source code and models have been made publicly available at https://github.com/CCF-Union/UXNet.
